content: Consent for vaccination can be obtained through a written consent form. Alternatively, verbal or implied consent procedures may be utilized. It is considered best practice to allow older children to express their agreement to vaccination, referred to as assent. Regardless of the consent method used, implementing opt-out protocols, where parents or children who do not wish to receive the vaccination must explicitly indicate their decision, is more efficient. Written consent procedures, however, require additional advance planning. Supplementary Immunization Activities (SIAs), also known as mass immunization campaigns, are a critical component of rubella and measles control and elimination strategies. The initial SIAs targeting a wide age range aim to significantly reduce rubella virus transmission, thereby protecting women of reproductive age (WRA) from rubella infection and the associated risk of congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Vaccination of WRA and healthcare workers is an essential part of this strategy. A separate guide focusing on SIAs for measles-rubella (MR) campaigns is under development by the World Health Organization (WHO). This guide will provide detailed instructions on planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of SIAs. In the meantime, a brief description of SIA-specific aspects is available in Annex 6. By 2014, 140 out of 194 WHO member states (72%) had introduced rubella-containing vaccines (RCV) into their national immunization programs, either as MR or measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccines. Member states report RCV coverage through the Joint Reporting Form (JRF) to WHO and UNICEF. Existing tally sheets used during immunization sessions must be updated to include RCV. Spaces currently designated for recording the first and second doses of measles vaccines can be replaced with spaces for MR1 and MR2. Vaccination cards, clinic immunization registers, reporting forms, and summary forms must also be updated to include RCV. Additionally, provisions should be made to record doses administered to older children and adults. To estimate RCV coverage, especially among WRA, countries may rely on administrative reports or conduct coverage surveys. In countries without registers for WRA, coverage surveys may be the only method to estimate RCV coverage. Serosurveys among women attending health facilities, such as antenatal clinics, can also be used to estimate protection against rubella. Rubella surveillance must be integrated with measles case-based surveillance. Initially, rubella cases may be identified by testing sera that are negative for measles. As countries establish rubella control or elimination goals, the surveillance system may be modified to include cases of fever and rash or suspected measles or rubella. Rubella surveillance includes two components: (1) case-based surveillance for rubella cases with laboratory confirmation and outbreak investigation, and (2) CRS surveillance at sentinel sites or during outbreak investigations. CRS surveillance should be established before or soon after RCV introduction to document the impact of the vaccination program in reducing CRS incidence. Rubella case definitions include: Suspected rubella case: Any patient of any age suspected by a healthcare worker to have rubella, particularly if presenting with fever, maculopapular rash, and cervical, suboccipital, or postauricular adenopathy, or arthralgia/arthritis. Clinically compatible rubella case: A case with maculopapular rash, fever, and one of arthritis/arthralgia or lymphadenopathy, without adequate clinical specimens or epidemiological linkage to a laboratory-confirmed rubella case. Laboratory-confirmed rubella case: A suspected case with positive laboratory results, such as rubella-specific IgM, a fourfold rise in IgG titers, or detection of rubella virus or RNA. Epidemiologically confirmed rubella case: A suspected case linked geographically and temporally to a laboratory-confirmed rubella case or another epidemiologically confirmed rubella case. Pregnant women exposed to or suspected of having rubella are of particular concern. They should undergo laboratory testing and be followed until delivery to assess pregnancy outcomes. If susceptible, they should be vaccinated postpartum. Testing should include rubella-specific IgM and, if available, IgG. Positive IgM results require counseling and follow-up. In low-incidence or near-elimination settings, additional laboratory evaluation is necessary to confirm rubella IgM results in pregnant women without a history of illness or contact with rubella-like illness. CRS surveillance is essential to monitor the effectiveness of rubella vaccination programs, detect affected infants, and provide early medical care. Rapid identification of infants with CRS ensures appropriate testing, entry into the CRS surveillance system, and infection control to prevent further spread. Infants with CRS may shed the virus for up to one year. CRS surveillance also facilitates early intervention for specific defects and allows for standardized regional and global reporting. CRS case definitions include: Suspected CRS case: Any infant under one year of age suspected by a healthcare worker to have CRS, particularly if presenting with heart disease, hearing impairment, or eye abnormalities such as cataracts, congenital glaucoma, or pigmentary retinopathy. CRS should also be suspected if the infant's mother had suspected or confirmed rubella during pregnancy, even if the infant shows no signs of CRS. Clinically confirmed CRS case: An infant diagnosed by a qualified physician with at least two complications from group (a) (e.g., cataracts, congenital glaucoma, congenital heart disease, hearing impairment, pigmentary retinopathy) or one from group (a) and one from group (b) (e.g., purpura, splenomegaly). Pregnancy outcomes for women with confirmed rubella infection during pregnancy should be recorded to understand the impact of rubella. Outcomes may include miscarriage, termination, stillbirth, fetal death, or infants born with CRS, congenital rubella infection (CRI), or no abnormalities. For pregnant women delivering at health facilities, the facility must be notified in advance to ensure the infant is isolated and evaluated for CRS, including laboratory testing.
